title: Why Amplifiers Lose Bass Explained Simply | PUC Electronics Class 12
description:
Aarav plays a song through a small amplifier. The singer is loud, but the deep drums and the high whistles are weak. Why does one amplifier boost some sounds better than others? We start with a rubber wall in a pipe (a capacitor) and a pipe with tiny leaks (hidden capacitance).

On a live breadboard we build a CE amplifier on voltage divider bias with an input coupling capacitor, an output coupling capacitor, a bypass capacitor and a load. A 10 mV wave at 1 kHz comes out as 1.5 V, upside down. Then we turn the frequency knob: at 20 Hz and at 1 MHz the oscilloscope shows the output shrinking. The frequency response curve shows the flat mid band, the low-frequency drop (capacitor reactance) and the high-frequency drop (junction and wiring capacitance), the 0.707 cut-offs f1 and f2 and the bandwidth. We derive r'e = 26 mV / I_E, r_c = R_C parallel R_L, A_v = -r_c / r'e and gain in decibels, then work an example, followed by the exam trap (at the cut-off the voltage gain falls to 0.707, the power to half), where it is asked, an original practice question with a full solution, and a formula card to screenshot.

This is Episode 67 of PUC Electronics, Class 12, Chapter 3: Transistor Amplifiers (Karnataka II PUC Electronics). Transistor amplifiers are not in the rationalised NCERT/CBSE Class 12 Physics book or the current ISC Physics syllabus, so this lesson follows the Karnataka PUC Electronics syllabus.
